newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: FIGURE SKATING-SKATERS FACE QUADRUPLE DILEMMA.
newsitem.headline: FIGURE SKATING-SKATERS FACE QUADRUPLE DILEMMA.

text.p: The world figure skating championships were a quad-free zone during the men's short programme on Wednesday.
But Thursday's free skate is expected to be littered with quadruple jumps with as many as 10 skaters attempting one.
At last year's championships in Edmonton, Alberta, Canadian Elvis Stojko was the only skater to include a quadruple jump in his repertoire.

But on Thursday the Malley Arena will see a deluge of attempts at a manoeuvre that just 12 months ago was considered an unnecessary risk but is now seen as almost essential to those harbouring serious gold medal aspirations.

All three Russians including gold medal contenders Alexei Urmanov, the Olympic champion, and Ilya Kulik, American Michael Weiss and Stojko have quads scheduled while five others have indicated they will attempt the jump.
"We have almost forced people into this," said Stojko's coach Dough Leigh. "We've raised the risk factor.
"We'll see who survives the test - whether it's now or whether it's next year in Nagano. We're on new turf now.
"It used to be, 'don't leave home without a triple Axel'. Now, it's 'if you want to be on the podium, having a quad is critical,'" added Leigh.

It was Stojko who again raised the stakes two weeks ago when he became the first skater to land a quadruple-triple jump combination in competition on his way to winning the Champions Series final in Hamilton, Ontario.
Now, the intriguing question being posed is whether you need a quad to land on top of the podium.

A growing number believe it must be part of the modern skater's arsenal but others, such as defending champion Todd Eldredge of the United States who has not attempted the jump in competition, are not convinced.
"I guess a lot of it will depend on what the other guys do," said Eldredge, second behind Urmanov and ahead of Kulik after the short programme. "I don't know whether I'll need one or not.
"I just want to skate as well tomorrow for two minutes more and do a lot more triples."
Fourth after the short, Stojko believes his ace-in-the-hole will be his quad combination.
But the muscular Canadian is more than aware it will take something more than seven aerial spins in two seconds to reclaim the title he won in 1994 and 1995.
"There's a whole programme involved," said Stojko. "But it's a great asset.
"If you do a clean performance with a quad I think you'll be up there. A quad is part of the full package now."
